Warmachine & Hordes Miniature Scale for 3D Printing

Warmachine sits at a stocky 30mm — the in-between scale that is neither true 28mm nor heroic 32mm. The heavily armored warjacks are big enough that FDM handles them well, but getting the infantry-and-jack pairing consistent takes a little planning.

Warmachine was originally marketed as 28mm but was reclassified to 30mm around the time Hordes launched. The miniatures are compatible in size with 28mm heroic ranges — the difference is subtle enough that mixing on the same table is common in casual play.

Publisher: Privateer Press·Base Sizes: 30mm, 40mm, 50mm

The 30mm scale gives warjacks physical presence that 28mm does not, so mixing sources means deciding whether your infantry should hit 30mm to match. I scale everything to a uniform 30mm baseline for a coherent force and keep that single number across an entire battle group.

Warjacks are chunky and print cleanly at broader profiles, which balances out the finer infantry work. I print the jacks at 0.2mm layers and the models at a finer profile, so my print time stays sane without sacrificing the faces and weapon detail on the characters.

Deep Dive: 30mm — the scale creep you cannot label

Warmachine launched as 28mm and Privateer Press now calls the range 30mm. Printing proxies means accepting that '30mm' is not a conversion target — it is a bracket between 28mm and 32mm.

28mm, 30mm, or Both?

Warmachine was originally marketed as 28mm and reclassified to 30mm around the time Hordes launched. The miniatures use chunky heroic proportions — exaggerated weapons and armor, beefy silhouettes. Both labels are accepted in the community, and the range's own models span the bracket depending on when they were sculpted.

Where Printed Proxies Land

Most STL files are labeled either "28mm heroic" or "32mm heroic." Warmachine's 30mm sits between the two. In practice I treat Warmachine as 28mm heroic when I print proxies, then verify with the caliper against a reference 'jack or infantry model. If a file runs big or small, I adjust by a touch and re-measure — the label is a starting point, not the answer.

The Bracket in Numbers

There is no validated "30mm" conversion in the matrix, so the two validated references that bracket the lane are the ones I use:

Conversion Formula Slicer %
Classic (28mm) → Heroic (32mm)32 ÷ 28114.3%
Heroic (32mm) → Classic (28mm)28 ÷ 3287.5%

Scaling a Warmachine proxy all the way to strict 32mm usually overshoots a real army — that step is the top of the bracket, not the middle.

FDM Settings for 'Jacks

Warmachine's bulky mechanical designs are forgiving on FDM — flat armor panels hide layer lines, and warjacks are big enough that I run a 0.4mm nozzle at 0.1mm layers for the machines. Heavy infantry and characters get a 0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm. The metal originals are heavy, so printed alternatives are noticeably lighter and easier to transport.

Common Warmachine Mistakes

  • Forcing a 30mm army to strict 32mm scale. Your proxies will read oversized next to the range — stay in the 28mm heroic lane.
  • Measuring to the top of a 'jack's cab. Eye level is the reference even on machines; the cab is usually a raised detail, not the scale point.
  • FDM on heavy-troop trim. The heavy troops have a lot of small trim that FDM softens first.

Printing these minis on FDM

Warjacks print well at a 0.4mm nozzle and 0.2mm layers. Infantry and characters get a 0.4mm nozzle at 0.08mm, or a 0.2mm nozzle for exposed faces. Scale the whole force to 30mm for consistency.

All settings tested on my Bambu Lab A1 Mini with PLA. Your printer may want something different — always print a test piece first.

Frequently Asked Questions

What scale is Warmachine?
Warmachine & Hordes is 30mm scale, stockier than 28mm with exaggerated armor and weapons.
Does scaling a Warmachine proxy to 32mm matter?
You can, but the range is designed at 30mm. Keeping everything at 30mm gives a more coherent force than guessing.
